payload.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
payload.holding: The Court held that the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for fixed/self-employed income based on standardized percentages, and the Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
payload.ratio: In motor accident compensation claims under Section 166 of the MV Act, the multiplier must be selected based on the age of the deceased rather than the claimants, future prospects apply to fixed-salary and self-employed individuals, and appellate courts are obligated under Order XLI Rule 33 and the concept of just compensation to correct and enhance inadequate awards.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

payload.holding: The Court held that where passengers carried in a goods vehicle or tractor are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither covered by statute nor by the insurance policy, the Claims Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct the insurance company to first pay the compensation and then recover it from the owner.

taken and percentage of disability is quite conservative if we may say so.

45. In the case of UNITED INDIA INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITD VS. VELUCHAMY, (2005 (1)
CTC 38), Division Bench of this Court has held that having regard to the nature of injuries, in
appropriate cases, Court can adopt multiplier method to award compensation for permanent
disability. The determination of the quantum must be liberal and not meagre. The entire future of
the claimant is now crippled and he is now confined to bed and incapacitated. The Tribunal has
taken the income of the claimant at Rs.4,500/- per month and rightly adopted multiplier the
method by adopting multiplier 16. In our considered view, the compensation of Rs.8,20,800/-
(Rs.4,500 x 12 x 16 x 95/100) awarded for the "permanent disability" is just and reasonable and the

46. Insofar as "pain and suffering", Tribunal has awarded only a sum of Rs.25,000/- and for "mental

compensation awarded for "pain and suffering", the compensation of Rs.75,000/- awarded under

nourishment" and "transport", the Tribunal has awarded Rs.1,000/- each and the same is
maintained. As pointed out, earlier, claimant has been continuously taking treatment and the
compensation of Rs.1,00,000/-awarded for actual loss of income is also reasonable and the same is
maintained. The Tribunal in fact could have awarded more compensation for future medical
expenses and attendant charges. Since there is no cross appeal/objection, we leave at that.

args.question: I act for the insurer and want to appeal the quantum, not liability. Which judgments support reducing an award on appeal, and which cut against me?

supporting.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
supporting.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'; only dependents count for calculating the deduction for personal expenses.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the claimants include non-dependent major children or other relatives who were not financially dependent on the deceased, the insurer can argue that the dependency deduction should be higher (1/2 instead of 1/3) and compensation reduced accordingly.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest precedent in the corpus for actually reducing quantum on appeal. The High Court recalculated the award by excluding non-dependent claimants from the dependency calculation, increasing the personal-expense deduction from 1/3 to 1/2, and reducing total compensation.
supporting.quote: That a legal representative, who was not dependent upon the deceased, is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'... Strength of the family of the deceased for the purpose of 'loss of dependency' in this case should have been and is being taken as two only and in applying the multiplier method, deduction towards personal expenses of the deceased would be half of the salary.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation from 9% to 7.5% per annum, reflecting falling interest rate trends.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at 9% or higher, the insurer can argue for reduction to 7.5% or lower based on prevailing bank rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: This directly supports reducing a component of the award (interest rate) on appeal. The court reduced interest from 9% to 7.5% citing falling interest rates. This is a clean, low-risk argument for partial reduction.
supporting.quote: Both the appeals are dismissed except with a modification in the rate of interest which we reduce and allow @7.5% only instead 9% per annum.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Where the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, no addition towards future prospects should be made. The court reduced compensation by removing the 50% future prospects addition.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the deceased was self-employed or on fixed wages without permanent employment, the insurer can argue that no future prospects addition should be made, reducing the multiplicand.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a strong precedent for reducing quantum where the Tribunal erroneously added future prospects for a self-employed or temporary worker. The court specifically held that for a deceased not in permanent/regular employment, no addition for future prospects is permissible.
supporting.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation to 6% per annum, reflecting the trend of falling interest rates.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at 7.5% or higher, the insurer can argue for reduction to 6% based on prevailing rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: Although the overall outcome in this case was adverse (compensation enhanced), the court reduced the interest rate from 7.5% to 6%. This supports a partial reduction argument on interest.
supporting.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest from 12% to 9% per annum in line with prevailing economic conditions.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at a rate higher than 9%, the insurer can argue for reduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the argument that interest rates on compensation awards should reflect prevailing economic conditions and can be reduced on appeal.
supporting.quote: The Apex Court... has held that, in view of the change in economy and policy of Reserve Bank of India and the prevalent rate of interest for fixed deposit by the nationalised banks, it would be reasonable to award interest at 9 per cent per annum.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: The appellate court can re-calculate compensation using minimum wages instead of the DC Rate where the deceased's income was not properly proved, and can adjust future prospects percentages.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal assessed income based on an inflated or unsubstantiated figure, the insurer can argue for re-assessment based on minimum wage schedules or more conservative income estimates.
supporting.why_it_matters: The court modified compensation by adjusting income assessment and future prospects percentages. While the overall outcome was mixed (some enhancements too), it shows the appellate court's willingness to re-examine quantum.
supporting.quote: The learned counsel for insurance company argued that the quantum of compensation awarded... is towards the higher side. The learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal... could not have considered his income as per the wages fixed for the employees of various Government departments, rather, the income of deceased should have been considered as provided under Minimum Wages Act.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, the appellate court can enhance compensation even in the absence of a cross-appeal or cross-objections by the claimant, because the court is duty-bound to award 'just compensation'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even if the insurer appeals only quantum, the court can enhance the award beyond what the Tribunal granted. The court here enhanced compensation from Rs. 4,00,000 to Rs. 5,99,000 while reducing interest — a net increase.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved a poor, illiterate claimant from an underdeveloped region, which the court expressly noted as a reason to invoke Order 41 Rule 33. If your claimants are not in a similarly vulnerable position, or if the Tribunal's award was already adequate, this can be distinguished. Also, the court's power under Order 41 Rule 33 is discretionary, not mandatory.
adverse.quote: Although there is neither any appeal against the award nor cross-objections, but still this Court needs to test whether the award was just... this Court is inclined to award just compensation by modifying the impugned award, primarily for the reason that the claimant is apparently a poor lady, not aware of her legal rights.

adverse.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
adverse.principle: The appellate court has power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal. The multiplier must be based on the deceased's age, and future prospects apply even to self-employed persons.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the court can enhance compensation on its own motion, and that the multiplier and future prospects must be applied correctly — potentially increasing the award if the Tribunal made errors favourable to the insurer.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved appeals by both claimants (for enhancement) and the insurer (claiming excess). The court was resolving conflicting precedents on multiplier and future prospects. If the Tribunal in your case applied the correct multiplier and future prospects per Pranay Sethi, this case does not support enhancement. The key is whether the Tribunal's calculation was already compliant with settled law.
adverse.quote: The Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: The appellate court can set aside a finding of contributory negligence and enhance compensation by adding future prospects (30% for government employee aged 40-50) and correcting improper deductions (VPF and festival advance should not be deducted from income).
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that if the Tribunal made any error adverse to the claimant (e.g., wrongly deducting savings, failing to add future prospects, or wrongly apportioning negligence), the appellate court can correct those errors and enhance compensation — even if the claimant did not cross-appeal.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on specific errors: the Tribunal deducted VPF and festival advance (which are part of income) and failed to add future prospects for a government employee. If the Tribunal in your case correctly computed income without such errors, this case is distinguishable. The enhancement here was driven by correcting clear legal errors, not by a general power to increase.
adverse.quote: The amounts i.e. Rs. 500/- towards V.P.F. and Rs. 150/- towards festival advance were the part of the income of the deceased and therefore the said amounts could have been deducted while calculating the income of the deceased available for the dependent family members.

adverse.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
adverse.principle: In cases of permanent disablement, compensation for loss of future earnings must account for functional disability in relation to the victim's vocation, not just the medical percentage of disability.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claimant has suffered a serious injury (especially amputation or similar), the opposing side will cite this to argue that the Tribunal's assessment of functional disability was too low and should be enhanced on appeal.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This was a claimant's appeal for enhancement, not an insurer's appeal. It applies only where the Tribunal ignored functional disability. If the Tribunal in your case properly assessed disability, this case does not support enhancement. Also, it concerns injury (not death) claims, which have different assessment principles.
adverse.quote: The Tribunal fell for error in ignoring the functional disability in reference to the loss of future prospective income of the applicant.

adverse.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1 Has Filed The Written Statement To ...
adverse.principle: When the deceased is below 40 years of age and in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the deceased was below 40 and in permanent employment, the opposing side will argue that 50% future prospects addition is mandatory per Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi, and if the Tribunal awarded less, the appellate court should enhance.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a Tribunal decision, not an appellate judgment, so it has limited precedential value. The principle is well-settled by the Supreme Court in Pranay Sethi. If the Tribunal already applied the correct percentage, this case adds nothing. If the Tribunal applied a lower percentage, the risk is real but the insurer should focus on whether the deceased truly had 'stable employment'.
adverse.quote: 50% of actual salary should be added to the actual salary income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below 40 years.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer's appeal against quantum can be dismissed where the Tribunal's award is found to be just and reasonable, and the burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the appellate court should not interfere with the Tribunal's quantum unless it is wholly arbitrary or perverse. The court here dismissed the insurer's appeal and confirmed the award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court confirmed the award because it found the Tribunal's assessment reasonable. If the insurer can point to specific errors in the Tribunal's calculation (wrong multiplier, wrong deduction, wrong income assessment), this case is distinguishable. The principle is that appellate interference requires demonstrable error, not mere disagreement.
adverse.quote: The appeal of the insurance company is dismissed, confirming the judgment and award passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal granting compensation of Rs. 4,17,500/- with interest.

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: An insurer without permission under Section 170 of the MV Act cannot challenge the quantum of compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that if the insurer did not obtain permission under Section 170 from the Tribunal, it is barred from challenging quantum on appeal. This is a procedural threshold issue.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The law on this point has evolved. In doc_018 (Oriental Insurance vs Rani), the court held that once the insurer is impleaded as a party respondent, it can contest on all grounds without being restricted to Section 149(2) defences. However, the position in doc_023 (an older 2005 decision) is more restrictive. The insurer should check whether it obtained Section 170 permission or was already a party respondent. If the insurer was already impleaded, the more liberal view in doc_018 applies.
adverse.quote: The Assurance Company cannot challenge the quantum of compensation without having permission under Section 170 of the Act.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: The appellate court can enhance compensation by adding future prospects (40% for a 22-year-old) even when the insurer appeals quantum and the claimants have not filed cross-objections, if the Tribunal's omission is a 'glaring mistake'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that if the Tribunal failed to add future prospects or applied the wrong percentage, the appellate court can and should correct this even in an insurer's appeal, resulting in enhancement.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court here said the omission of future prospects was a 'glaring mistake' that could not be ignored. If the Tribunal in your case correctly applied future prospects, this case is distinguishable. The risk is real only if the Tribunal made an error that benefits the insurer.
adverse.quote: There is a glaring mistake that the Tribunal has not considered future prospects while calculating the quantum of compensation and the same cannot be ignored.

priority_arguments: 1. Dependency deduction: Argue that non-dependent claimants (major children, gainfully employed relatives) should be excluded from the dependency calculation, increasing the personal-expense deduction from 1/3 to 1/2 (per doc_007 - Harpreet Singh).

2. Future prospects: Argue that no future prospects addition should be made if the deceased was self-employed or in temporary/irregular employment (per doc_033 - Satto). Even if future prospects apply, ensure the correct percentage is used per Pranay Sethi (40% for under 40, 30% for 40-50, 15% for 50-60, 0% for above 60; for self-employed: 10% for under 40, nil for above 40).
3. Interest rate reduction: Argue for reduction of interest from 9% or higher to 6-7.5% based on prevailing bank rates (per doc_004, doc_023, doc_034).
4. Income assessment: Challenge inflated income assessments. Argue for minimum wage-based income where the deceased's actual income is not properly proved (per doc_001 - Neelam Devi).

5. Multiplier: Verify the Tribunal applied the correct multiplier per Sarla Verma (deceased's age-based, not claimant's age). If a wrong multiplier was used that favours the claimant, argue for correction.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without specific facts. Use compute_quantum tool with actual figures.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The insurer should first compute the 'correct' compensation using the compute_quantum tool with the actual facts (income, age, dependents, employment type). Compare this with the Tribunal's award. Any excess is the reduction target. The strongest arguments are: (1) removing future prospects for non-permanent employment, (2) increasing dependency deduction for non-dependent claimants, (3) reducing interest rate.
risks: HIGH RISK: The appellate court may enhance compensation under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC even without a cross-appeal by the claimant (doc_004, doc_019). This is the single biggest risk of appealing quantum alone.
HIGH RISK: If the Tribunal made any error adverse to the claimant (wrong deduction, omitted future prospects, wrong multiplier), the court will correct it and enhance the award (doc_006, doc_001).

HIGH RISK: The insurer may be procedurally barred from challenging quantum if it did not obtain Section 170 MV Act permission from the Tribunal (doc_023). However, this is mitigated if the insurer was already a party respondent (doc_018).
MEDIUM RISK: The court may find the Tribunal's award reasonable and dismiss the appeal with costs (doc_018).
MEDIUM RISK: If the deceased was below 40 and in permanent employment, 50% future prospects is mandatory, and any attempt to reduce it will fail (doc_041).
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Proceed with the appeal but ONLY if: (1) the insurer obtained Section 170 permission or was already impleaded as a party respondent; (2) there is a specific, demonstrable error in the Tribunal's calculation (wrong multiplier, wrong dependency deduction, improper future prospects for non-permanent employee, inflated income); and (3) the Tribunal's award is clearly excessive compared to a correct calculation. File the appeal specifically on quantum grounds, but be prepared for the risk of enhancement. Consider not appealing if the excess is marginal and the enhancement risk is high.

caveats: This corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly on the question of when an insurer can successfully appeal quantum. The highest authority is High Court judgments. The Pranay Sethi framework (which governs multiplier, future prospects, and conventional heads) is cited in several judgments but is not itself in the corpus.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Madras
payload.holding: The Court held that while the driver did not possess a specific endorsement to drive a heavy goods vehicle (having only a light motor vehicle licence with a transport vehicle endorsement), in third-party insurance claims, the insurer must indemnify the victim and is entitled to a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.

args.question: I act for the insurer and want to appeal the quantum, not liability. Which judgments support reducing an award on appeal, and which cut against me?

supporting.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
supporting.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'; only dependents count for calculating the deduction for personal expenses.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the claimants include non-dependent major children or other relatives who were not financially dependent on the deceased, the insurer can argue that the dependency deduction should be higher (1/2 instead of 1/3) and compensation reduced accordingly.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest precedent in the corpus for actually reducing quantum on appeal. The High Court recalculated the award by excluding non-dependent claimants from the dependency calculation, increasing the personal-expense deduction from 1/3 to 1/2, and reducing total compensation.
supporting.quote: That a legal representative, who was not dependent upon the deceased, is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'... Strength of the family of the deceased for the purpose of 'loss of dependency' in this case should have been and is being taken as two only and in applying the multiplier method, deduction towards personal expenses of the deceased would be half of the salary.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation from 9% to 7.5% per annum, reflecting falling interest rate trends.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at 9% or higher, the insurer can argue for reduction to 7.5% or lower based on prevailing bank rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: This directly supports reducing a component of the award (interest rate) on appeal. The court reduced interest from 9% to 7.5% citing falling interest rates. This is a clean, low-risk argument for partial reduction.
supporting.quote: Both the appeals are dismissed except with a modification in the rate of interest which we reduce and allow @7.5% only instead 9% per annum.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Where the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, no addition towards future prospects should be made. The court reduced compensation by removing the 50% future prospects addition.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the deceased was self-employed or on fixed wages without permanent employment, the insurer can argue that no future prospects addition should be made, reducing the multiplicand.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a strong precedent for reducing quantum where the Tribunal erroneously added future prospects for a self-employed or temporary worker. The court specifically held that for a deceased not in permanent/regular employment, no addition for future prospects is permissible.
supporting.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation to 6% per annum, reflecting the trend of falling interest rates.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at 7.5% or higher, the insurer can argue for reduction to 6% based on prevailing rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: Although the overall outcome in this case was adverse (compensation enhanced), the court reduced the interest rate from 7.5% to 6%. This supports a partial reduction argument on interest.
supporting.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The appellate court can reduce the rate of interest from 12% to 9% per annum in line with prevailing economic conditions.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal awarded interest at a rate higher than 9%, the insurer can argue for reduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the argument that interest rates on compensation awards should reflect prevailing economic conditions and can be reduced on appeal.
supporting.quote: The Apex Court... has held that, in view of the change in economy and policy of Reserve Bank of India and the prevalent rate of interest for fixed deposit by the nationalised banks, it would be reasonable to award interest at 9 per cent per annum.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: The appellate court can re-calculate compensation using minimum wages instead of the DC Rate where the deceased's income was not properly proved, and can adjust future prospects percentages.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the Tribunal assessed income based on an inflated or unsubstantiated figure, the insurer can argue for re-assessment based on minimum wage schedules or more conservative income estimates.
supporting.why_it_matters: The court modified compensation by adjusting income assessment and future prospects percentages. While the overall outcome was mixed (some enhancements too), it shows the appellate court's willingness to re-examine quantum.
supporting.quote: The learned counsel for insurance company argued that the quantum of compensation awarded... is towards the higher side. The learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal... could not have considered his income as per the wages fixed for the employees of various Government departments, rather, the income of deceased should have been considered as provided under Minimum Wages Act.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, the appellate court can enhance compensation even in the absence of a cross-appeal or cross-objections by the claimant, because the court is duty-bound to award 'just compensation'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even if the insurer appeals only quantum, the court can enhance the award beyond what the Tribunal granted. The court here enhanced compensation from Rs. 4,00,000 to Rs. 5,99,000 while reducing interest — a net increase.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved a poor, illiterate claimant from an underdeveloped region, which the court expressly noted as a reason to invoke Order 41 Rule 33. If your claimants are not in a similarly vulnerable position, or if the Tribunal's award was already adequate, this can be distinguished. Also, the court's power under Order 41 Rule 33 is discretionary, not mandatory.
adverse.quote: Although there is neither any appeal against the award nor cross-objections, but still this Court needs to test whether the award was just... this Court is inclined to award just compensation by modifying the impugned award, primarily for the reason that the claimant is apparently a poor lady, not aware of her legal rights.

adverse.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
adverse.principle: The appellate court has power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal. The multiplier must be based on the deceased's age, and future prospects apply even to self-employed persons.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the court can enhance compensation on its own motion, and that the multiplier and future prospects must be applied correctly — potentially increasing the award if the Tribunal made errors favourable to the insurer.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved appeals by both claimants (for enhancement) and the insurer (claiming excess). The court was resolving conflicting precedents on multiplier and future prospects. If the Tribunal in your case applied the correct multiplier and future prospects per Pranay Sethi, this case does not support enhancement. The key is whether the Tribunal's calculation was already compliant with settled law.
adverse.quote: The Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: The appellate court can set aside a finding of contributory negligence and enhance compensation by adding future prospects (30% for government employee aged 40-50) and correcting improper deductions (VPF and festival advance should not be deducted from income).
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that if the Tribunal made any error adverse to the claimant (e.g., wrongly deducting savings, failing to add future prospects, or wrongly apportioning negligence), the appellate court can correct those errors and enhance compensation — even if the claimant did not cross-appeal.
